title: Looper, Handler, MessageQueue
scopeHtml: Scope: the per-thread message loop model, Handler/Message mechanics, HandlerThread, time bases, view.post and thread checks. Frame mechanics are M2 (Q131+), Doze/alarm policy is B1.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how Looper, MessageQueue, Handler and Message work together. Why does the main thread never "finish"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Almost every Android threading bug (leaks, ANRs, wrong-thread crashes) is a misunderstanding of this model. It separates people who memorized "UI thread" from people who know what the thread is actually doing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every thread that wants to receive work has one Looper, which owns one MessageQueue. The Looper runs an infinite loop: take the next due Message off the queue, hand it to the Handler it targets, repeat; when nothing is due, the thread sleeps in native code. A Handler is the front door: any thread calls handler.post() or sendMessage() to enqueue work, and the work later runs on the thread that owns the Looper. The main thread never finishes because ActivityThread.main() ends by calling Looper.loop(), and everything the framework does there (lifecycle callbacks, input, traversals, broadcasts) arrives as messages.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Four pieces, one thread:

 any thread                        thread that owns the Looper
 ----------                        ---------------------------
 handler.post(r) ----enqueue---->  MessageQueue (linked list sorted by 'when')
 handler.sendMessage(m)                   |
                                          v   Looper.loop(): for(;;) { m = queue.next(); ... }
                                  Looper -- m.target.dispatchMessage(m) --> Handler on the looper's thread
  • Message: a small object holding what, arg1, arg2, obj, optional callback (Runnable), a target (the Handler) and when (a time in SystemClock.uptimeMillis() base).
  • MessageQueue: a singly linked list ordered by when. It is not a priority queue and not a FIFO; a message with an earlier when is inserted ahead of later ones.
  • Looper: one per thread, stored in a ThreadLocal. Looper.loop() calls queue.next(), which blocks (epoll via nativePollOnce) until a message is due, then dispatches it.
  • Handler: binds to one Looper at construction. It does not own a thread; it is a producer-side handle plus a consumer-side callback (handleMessage / the Runnable).

The main thread: ActivityThread.main() calls Looper.prepareMainLooper(), creates the ActivityThread and its inner H handler, attaches to system_server, then calls Looper.loop(). onCreate, onResume, Service.onStartCommand, BroadcastReceiver.onReceive, ViewRootImpl.performTraversals (via Choreographer) are all just messages dispatched by that loop. If loop() ever returned, the process would exit; the framework throws RuntimeException("Main thread loop unexpectedly exited").

Consequence: one thread runs one message at a time. A slow onReceive delays the next frame. There is no preemption between messages.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.Handler
import android.os.Looper

val main = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())

fun deliverFromWorker() {
    Thread {
        val result = heavyWork()          // runs on worker
        main.post { render(result) }      // runs later on the main thread's loop
    }.start()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the Handler "is" a thread or "runs" the work. It only enqueues; the Looper's thread executes.
  • Believing the queue is FIFO. Delayed messages sort by when; a postDelayed(5000) does not block a later post().
  • Assuming the Looper preempts a long message. It cannot; the next message waits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can one thread have two Loopers? → No. Looper.prepare() twice throws "Only one Looper may be created per thread". Many Handlers can share one Looper.
  2. Can two threads share one Looper/queue? → Yes, a Handler can be created from any thread with a given Looper; that is how worker threads post to main.
  3. What does the main thread do when the queue is empty? → nativePollOnce parks the thread in epoll_wait (no CPU) until a message becomes due or a file descriptor event (input channel, vsync) fires.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists the four classes. The senior adds: the queue is a time-sorted list, the loop is single-message-at-a-time with no preemption, the thread sleeps in epoll (not a busy loop), and framework callbacks are themselves messages, so "blocking the main thread" literally means "delaying the next message".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Every "UI is janky after a sync finishes" bug is a worker posting 500 main.post {} calls that each do small work, starving the frame messages queued behind them.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between handler.post(Runnable) and handler.sendMessage(Message)? When both a Handler.Callback and handleMessage exist, who runs first?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know a Runnable is just a Message with a callback field, and that you can read old Handler-based code without guessing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: post(Runnable) wraps the Runnable into a Message via getPostMessage (callback field set, what unused) and enqueues it; sendMessage enqueues a message the Handler later decodes by what. They share one queue and one ordering rule. On dispatch: if msg.callback is set, run that Runnable and stop; otherwise if a Handler.Callback was passed to the constructor, call it; if it returns true the message is consumed, if false fall through to handleMessage.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Handler.dispatchMessage:

dispatchMessage(msg):
  if (msg.callback != null)        -> msg.callback.run()           // post(Runnable) path
  else:
     if (mCallback != null && mCallback.handleMessage(msg)) -> return   // consumed
     handleMessage(msg)                                            // subclass override

All send/post variants funnel into enqueueMessage(queue, msg, uptimeMillis), which sets msg.target = this and, if the handler is async, msg.setAsynchronous(true). Variants differ only in the when:

API when
post, sendMessage now
postDelayed(r, d), sendMessageDelayed uptimeMillis() + max(d, 0)
postAtTime(r, t) absolute uptimeMillis base t
postAtFrontOfQueue 0 (ahead of everything, including already-due messages)

what + arg1/arg2/obj suit state-machine style handlers and Messenger IPC (Messages are Parcelable only for Messenger, and obj must be a Parcelable framework class cross-process). Lambdas are fine for in-process code.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.Handler
import android.os.Looper
import android.os.Message

private const val MSG_TICK = 1

class Ticker : Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) {
    override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
        if (msg.what == MSG_TICK) {
            // do tick
            sendEmptyMessageDelayed(MSG_TICK, 1_000)
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the deprecated no-arg Handler() constructor (deprecated API 30): it binds to the current thread's Looper and crashes or silently binds to the wrong thread. Always pass a Looper.
  • Forgetting Handler.Callback returning true swallows the message; returning false still reaches handleMessage.
  • Using postAtFrontOfQueue casually; it can starve already-due work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would you prefer what-based messages over Runnables? → They can be cancelled/deduplicated with removeMessages(what) / hasMessages(what) without holding a Runnable reference.
  2. Is delivery order guaranteed for equal when? → Yes, insertion order is preserved for equal when (new message goes after existing ones with when <= its own).
  3. Can sendMessage fail? → It returns false if the Looper is quitting; the message is recycled and a warning "sending message to a Handler on a dead thread" is logged.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "post takes a Runnable, sendMessage takes a Message." Senior: knows post is sugar over Message.callback, the exact dispatch precedence, that when is uptime-based, and that the no-arg constructor is a latent bug.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash only in a library's background thread: Handler() created on a thread without a Looper (Can't create handler inside thread ... that has not called Looper.prepare()).

questions.promptHtml: How do you create your own Looper on a plain Thread? What happens if you create a Handler on a thread without one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Verifies you understand that "has a Looper" is an opt-in per-thread property, not something every thread gets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Call Looper.prepare() (creates the Looper and its queue, stores it in a ThreadLocal), create Handlers, then call Looper.loop(), which blocks forever; to stop, call looper.quit() from any thread. Creating a Handler() on a thread with no Looper throws RuntimeException: Can't create handler inside thread ... that has not called Looper.prepare(). In practice use HandlerThread rather than hand-rolling this.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Looper.prepare() -> sThreadLocal.set(new Looper(true)). A second call on the same thread throws.
  • Looper.myLooper() returns the calling thread's Looper or null. Looper.getMainLooper() returns the main one from any thread.
  • Looper.loop() takes the thread's Looper, then for(;;) calls queue.next(). next() returning null means "queue quit"; loop returns. Any code after loop() runs only after quit.
  • Handler constructor: mLooper = looper; mQueue = looper.mQueue. With no-arg constructor it calls Looper.myLooper() and throws if null. Hence the crash message.
  • Ordering trap: a Handler created before prepare() fails; a Handler created after prepare() but before loop() is fine, and messages posted to it before loop() starts simply wait in the queue.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.Handler
import android.os.Looper

class Worker : Thread("worker") {
    @Volatile lateinit var handler: Handler
    override fun run() {
        Looper.prepare()
        handler = Handler(Looper.myLooper()!!)
        Looper.loop()            // blocks until quit()
        // cleanup after quit
    }
}
// Race: handler is not set until run() reaches that line. HandlerThread solves this (see Q112).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading worker.handler right after start(); it may not be initialized yet (race). This is the classic reason HandlerThread exists.
  • Doing Looper.prepare() on a thread-pool thread you do not own; the pool thread then never returns to its pool loop.
  • Forgetting to quit: the thread (and everything it references) lives forever.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a coroutine or Executor thread not use Handler() directly? → Those threads have no Looper unless you prepare one; they run their own task loops.
  2. How does the main thread get its Looper? → ActivityThread.main() calls Looper.prepareMainLooper().
  3. How would you assert you are on the main thread cheaply? → Looper.getMainLooper().isCurrentThread (API 23+) or Looper.myLooper() == Looper.getMainLooper().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names prepare and loop. Senior: explains the ThreadLocal, the init race, quit semantics, and says "I would not hand-roll this; I would use HandlerThread or coroutines".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK crash Can't create handler inside thread Thread[pool-3-thread-1] appeared only when the host app initialised the SDK from an executor instead of the main thread.

questions.promptHtml: What is a HandlerThread, when would you still use it today, and how do you shut it down correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the serialized-work-with-a-Looper primitive and its lifecycle pitfalls (leaks, startup race, quit semantics).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HandlerThread is a Thread that sets up a Looper in run() and exposes it via getLooper(), which blocks until the Looper is ready, so there is no startup race. Work posted through a Handler on it runs serially, in time order, on one background thread. I use it for ordered, long-lived single-thread work (sensor/camera callbacks, a serialized disk writer, Bluetooth/GATT callbacks that need a Looper). Shutdown is quitSafely() (delivers already-due messages, drops future-delayed ones) or quit() (drops everything pending); and I must do it, or the thread leaks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• run(): Looper.prepare(); synchronized(this){ mLooper = Looper.myLooper(); notifyAll(); } onLooperPrepared(); Looper.loop();. getLooper() waits on that monitor if the thread is alive and mLooper is still null.
  • Serial execution: messages dispatch one at a time, so no locking is needed for state owned by that thread; but one slow message delays all others.
  • quit(): removes all pending messages, next() returns null, loop() returns, thread ends. quitSafely() (API 18): removes only messages whose when is in the future; already-due ones still run. Both are idempotent-ish: posting afterwards returns false.
  • Priority: HandlerThread(name, priority) takes a Process.THREAD_PRIORITY_* value (nice-style), not the java.lang.Thread priority.
  • Today: many cases are better served by Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() or Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1). HandlerThread remains right when an Android API requires a Handler/Looper (camera2 callbacks, SensorManager.registerListener(.., handler), Messenger, BluetoothGatt callbacks on some APIs).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.Handler
import android.os.HandlerThread
import android.os.Process

class SensorPipeline {
    private val thread = HandlerThread("sensor-io", Process.THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND).apply { start() }
    val handler = Handler(thread.looper)   // looper is non-null after start() because getLooper() blocks

    fun release() {
        thread.quitSafely()
        // optional: thread.join() off the main thread if you must wait
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Never quitting: every call creates a new HandlerThread (see the post-incident scenario Q126).
  • Calling thread.looper before start(): returns null.
  • Using join() on the main thread after quit; it can block while a message is mid-run.
  • Doing blocking I/O on a HandlerThread shared with latency-sensitive work (head-of-line blocking).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. quit() vs quitSafely()? → quit drops all pending; quitSafely runs due messages first, drops future ones.
  2. Is HandlerThread thread-safe for state? → Yes if only that thread touches the state; the message queue is the synchronization.
  3. How would you replace HandlerThread with coroutines while keeping ordering? → A single-threaded dispatcher (limitedParallelism(1)), but note coroutines may interleave at suspension points; ordering is per resume, not per launch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "a thread with a Looper." Senior: mentions the getLooper() handshake, quit semantics, priority constants, head-of-line blocking, and when a single-thread dispatcher is the better tool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A camera feature held a HandlerThread per screen open; 400 opens in a day leaked 400 threads, ending in pthread_create failed OOM.

questions.promptHtml: What clock does postDelayed use? Compare uptimeMillis, elapsedRealtime and currentTimeMillis, and say when each is right.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reveals whether you understand why delayed callbacks "drift" when the screen is off and why measuring durations with wall-clock time is wrong.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Handler delays are based on SystemClock.uptimeMillis(), which counts time since boot excluding deep sleep (when the CPU is suspended). elapsedRealtime() counts since boot including deep sleep and is the right clock for measuring real elapsed time. currentTimeMillis() is wall clock, which the user or network can change, so it is wrong for measuring intervals. So a postDelayed(10 min) when the device deep-sleeps for 8 minutes still has most of its delay left when the device wakes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Clock Counts deep sleep? Can jump? Use for
SystemClock.uptimeMillis() No No Handler scheduling, in-process timing while awake
SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() / elapsedRealtimeNanos() Yes No Real elapsed time, AlarmManager ELAPSED_REALTIME*, "session lasted N seconds"
System.currentTimeMillis() Yes Yes (user/NTP/timezone-independent but settable) Human timestamps, calendars
System.nanoTime() Platform-dependent; on Android it is CLOCK_MONOTONIC (stops in suspend) No Microbenchmarks

Why the Handler uses uptime: the MessageQueue epoll_wait timeout is computed in the monotonic clock; a suspended CPU executes nothing, so the loop cannot wake itself. When the device wakes (alarm, push, user), next() re-checks when against uptime; messages whose when has passed fire immediately, late by the sleep amount in wall-clock terms.

Rule: a Handler delay means "at least N ms of awake time from now". It is not a promise of wall time. For wall-time deadlines in the background you need AlarmManager (RTC or ELAPSED_REALTIME wakeups, see the B1 chunk) or WorkManager.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.SystemClock

// Wrong: wall clock can jump, and the user can change it
val start = System.currentTimeMillis()

// Right: real elapsed time including sleep
val t0 = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()
// ... later
val elapsedMs = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() - t0

// Handler.postAtTime takes an *uptime* timestamp
handler.postAtTime({ doIt() }, SystemClock.uptimeMillis() + 5_000)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing currentTimeMillis() plus delay to postAtTime; wrong base, so it fires essentially never or immediately.
  • Persisting uptimeMillis or elapsedRealtime across reboot; they reset at boot.
  • Measuring "time in app" with currentTimeMillis and getting negative values after a clock change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Thread.sleep count sleep time? → It also uses the monotonic clock, so it too stretches over deep sleep.
  2. How do you survive a reboot with an elapsed-time based timer? → Store the wall-clock target, recompute at boot (BOOT_COMPLETED), and schedule an alarm.
  3. Why does postDelayed(1000) often fire at 1000-1016 ms and not 1000 exactly? → The message is only eligible at when; it dispatches after the current message finishes and the loop wakes, so delay is a lower bound.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "uptime vs real time". Senior: ties it to epoll timeouts and CPU suspend, calls delays a lower bound, and picks AlarmManager/WorkManager for wall-time guarantees.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "session timeout after 30 minutes" using postDelayed never logged users out of backgrounded phones until they next unlocked them.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly does view.post { } do? Why does view.post { view.width } give a real width in onCreate when view.width directly gives 0?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of how attach, traversal and the main queue interact; a common source of "size is 0" bugs and leaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the view is attached to a window, View.post posts to the main Handler (the AttachInfo's handler). If it is not attached yet, the Runnable is parked in the view's own RunQueue and replayed when the view is attached, posted to that handler during the first traversal, after that traversal's measure and layout have run. So it runs after layout, which is why width is non-zero. It returns false and does nothing useful if the Looper is quitting.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
View.post(action):

attachInfo = mAttachInfo
if (attachInfo != null) return attachInfo.mHandler.post(action)
getRunQueue().post(action)   // per-view HandlerActionQueue (API 24+)
return true
  • In onCreate, the view tree has been inflated but ViewRootImpl does not exist yet; the first traversal happens after onResume (handleResumeActivity -> wm.addView -> scheduleTraversals).
  • In performTraversals for the first pass: host.dispatchAttachedToWindow(...) then getRunQueue().executeActions(mAttachInfo.mHandler) (this call hands the queued actions to the handler via post), and only then performMeasure / performLayout run in the same traversal. The queued actions run as separate messages after the current traversal message finishes, so layout is done.
  • Pre API 24, the pending-run queue was a static per-thread queue in ViewRootImpl, and posting from a view never attached could run on the wrong view's ViewRootImpl or be dropped; the per-view HandlerActionQueue fixed that. Mention this only if asked.
  • If the view is never attached (e.g. inflated and discarded), the Runnable is never run and holds the view in memory only as long as the view itself lives.
  • Not the same as doOnPreDraw / ViewTreeObserver.OnGlobalLayoutListener, which fire during traversal and must be removed manually.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import androidx.core.view.doOnLayout

override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.main)
    val v = findViewById<View>(R.id.card)
    Log.d("T", "direct=${v.width}")            // 0
    v.post { Log.d("T", "posted=${v.width}") } // real width
    v.doOnLayout { /* preferred: runs immediately if already laid out */ }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using view.post as a general "do it later" tool; ordering relative to other messages is not guaranteed beyond "after the first traversal".
  • Reading size in post after a configuration change when the view was detached; check isAttachedToWindow.
  • Assuming it runs before the first frame is drawn; the first frame may already be on screen.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. view.post vs doOnLayout? → doOnLayout runs inline if already laid out and not requested; post always defers a message.
  2. Does post from a background thread work? → Yes for an attached view (the AttachInfo handler is the main handler); that is why it is thread-safe, unlike direct view mutations.
  3. Why can a posted Runnable leak the Activity? → The Runnable captures this; if the view is detached and never re-attached, the RunQueue keeps it until the view dies; with delayed posts the queue holds it for the delay.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "post runs after layout." Senior: explains attached vs detached branches, why it is after layout (message after the first traversal), and prefers doOnLayout/doOnPreDraw with cleanup.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tooltip positioned using view.post showed at (0,0) on tablets when the view was inside a fragment not yet attached, because the Runnable ran before the fragment's view hit the window.

questions.contextHtml:
A profile screen (about 2M DAU) loads a user over Retrofit via a plain Thread. QA on the debug build sees nothing; in production Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions crashing, only on some devices and mostly when the network is fast:

android.view.ViewRootImpl$CalledFromWrongThreadException:
  Only the original thread that created a view hierarchy can touch its views.
    at android.view.ViewRootImpl.checkThread(ViewRootImpl.java:9006)
    at android.view.ViewRootImpl.requestLayout(ViewRootImpl.java:1900)
    at android.view.View.requestLayout(View.java:25000)
    at android.widget.TextView.setText(TextView.java:6000)
    at com.app.ProfileActivity$load$1.run(ProfileActivity.kt:42)
class ProfileActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var name: TextView

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.profile)
        name = findViewById(R.id.name)
        Thread {
            val user = api.getUser().execute().body()!!   // sometimes served from OkHttp cache in ~3 ms
            name.text = user.name
        }.start()
    }
}

A teammate says: "it works in most runs, so it can't be a threading bug."
questions.promptHtml: Why does this crash only sometimes, and what is the correct fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "You can't touch UI from a background thread, use runOnUiThread." True but misses why it passes on many runs, and why a fast cache hit is the failing case; also fixes the symptom while leaving lifecycle leaks (thread outliving the Activity).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the crash correlate with cache hits or slow devices? (tells me about timing relative to attach). Is the thread tied to a lifecycle? Are we on targetSdk where view mutations pre-attach are tolerated? Any other writers to name?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix by posting the UI update to the main thread (runOnUiThread or name.post) and guard on isFinishing/isDestroyed. Ship behind a staged rollout; the crash is a hard exception, not data loss, so a quick patch is safe.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Thread-check passes while the view is not yet attached, so slow runs sometimes survive; (b) setText that does not request layout/invalidate skips the check; (c) a different race (Activity destroyed). The red herring: "network is flaky".
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with a fake OkHttp interceptor returning instantly vs one with a 2 s delay; check Crashlytics breakdown by "time since onCreate" if logged. Log name.isAttachedToWindow at the write.
  5. Root cause: ViewRootImpl.checkThread() compares Thread.currentThread() with the thread that created the ViewRootImpl. The ViewRootImpl is created when the window is added, after onResume. Before that, View.mParent is null, so requestLayout() and invalidate() never reach ViewRootImpl and nothing checks the thread. A slow network means the write lands after attach, so it crashes; a 3 ms cache hit lands in the gap between onCreate and the first traversal (attach), so it silently succeeds. It is timing, not luck. Some mutations also take paths with no layout request, which is why the framework docs only promise the check, not that every wrong-thread call throws.
  6. Fix: short-term runOnUiThread { name.text = ... }. Long-term: stop using raw threads; lifecycleScope.launch { val user = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { api.getUser() }; name.text = user.name }, with the repository in a ViewModel and state collected via repeatOnLifecycle.
  7. Prevention: StrictMode is not enough for this; add a lint/Detekt rule banning Thread {} in UI classes, add an instrumented test with a synchronous fake API, and @MainThread/@WorkerThread annotations (lint checks them).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not catch the exception, which hides the bug and leaves inconsistent view state. I would not add Thread.sleep or delay hacks. I would not claim view.post alone fixes lifetime issues; the Activity can be gone by then.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does Toast.makeText(...).show() from a background thread throw? → It does not hit ViewRootImpl.checkThread (the toast is shown by the system), but Toast.makeText needs a Looper on the calling thread (it throws "Can't toast on a thread that has not called Looper.prepare()" on threads without one), so post it to main anyway.
  • Why is ProgressBar.setProgress allowed off-thread? → ProgressBar has documented thread-safe setProgress implemented by posting a refresh runnable; it is a deliberate exception.
  • Can you create a view hierarchy off the main thread? → Yes, with its own Looper (the check is per hierarchy creator thread), but it is fragile; avoid.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A release passed QA for two weeks because the QA backend was slow enough that every write landed after attach; a CDN cache change cut the response to 5 ms and the crash rate jumped from 0 to 0.4% overnight with no app change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says "use AsyncTask/runOnUiThread" with no explanation of intermittency.
  • Hire: explains the checkThread comes from ViewRootImpl, so pre-attach writes are unchecked, and fixes with main-thread dispatch plus lifecycle scoping.
  • Strong hire: adds the cache-timing explanation, lint/annotation prevention, a deterministic repro, and refuses to swallow the exception.

questions.contextHtml:
A weather app's DashboardActivity shows a refresh countdown. LeakCanary (debug) reports on every rotation:

┬───
│ GC Root: Thread (main) -> MessageQueue
├─ android.os.MessageQueue
│    ↓ MessageQueue.mMessages
├─ android.os.Message
│    ↓ Message.target
├─ DashboardActivity$refreshHandler$1   (anonymous Handler)
│    ↓ this$0
╰→ DashboardActivity (leaked, destroyed)
class DashboardActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val refreshHandler = object : Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) {
        override fun handleMessage(msg: Message) {
            tick()
            sendEmptyMessageDelayed(0, 60_000)
        }
    }
    override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); refreshHandler.sendEmptyMessageDelayed(0, 60_000) }
    override fun onStop() { super.onStop() /* forgot to stop */ }
}

Prod: Activity retains a 6 MB bitmap graph; 8% of low-RAM users (2 GB devices) hit OOM after ~12 rotations. Rotation is exactly the trigger the PM wants kept working.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this leak, how bad is it, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the Handler static with a WeakReference." That helps with the Handler itself but not if the message keeps re-arming forever, and it misses the lifecycle cause (never cancelled).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the loop self-rearming (here yes)? Does the leak show only on rotation or also on back? How long until it stops by itself? What objects does the Activity hold? On which devices does it OOM?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cancel the callback in onStop: refreshHandler.removeCallbacksAndMessages(null). One-line hotfix, safe.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Pending delayed Message references the Handler which references the Activity (anonymous inner class captures this$0); (b) the re-arming loop means the chain never ends; (c) something else (static singleton listener). The LeakCanary trace answers (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary trace (above), Android Studio heap dump for DashboardActivity instance count after 10 rotations, adb shell dumpsys meminfo <pkg> "Activities" count.
  5. Root cause: Message.target points to the Handler; the main MessageQueue is a GC root via the main thread; the anonymous Handler holds an implicit reference to its outer Activity. A message scheduled 60 s out, which re-posts itself on every fire, keeps the whole Activity alive indefinitely, not just for 60 s. Each rotation adds another leaked Activity because onStart of the new instance starts its own loop, and the old loop keeps firing.
  6. Fix: Short-term: removeCallbacksAndMessages(null) in onStop. Long-term: remove Handlers for periodic UI work: lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { while (true) { tick(); delay(60_000) } } }, which cancels automatically on stop, or move the ticking into the ViewModel. If a Handler is unavoidable, make it a static/top-level class with a WeakReference<Activity> and still remove callbacks, because messages otherwise accumulate.
  7. Prevention: Lint HandlerLeak (it warns about exactly this) treated as error in CI; LeakCanary in debug; a rotation test in the e2e suite that asserts Debug.countInstancesOfClass-style or leak detector pass; review rule: no inner Handler in components with a shorter lifetime than the Looper.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't just use WeakReference and call it fixed; the work keeps firing for a screen nobody sees (battery, tick on dead UI). Also I wouldn't largeHeap the leak away.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does a Handler on a HandlerThread leak the Activity too? → Yes, if it captures it; the thread's queue is the root instead of the main one.
  • Is Handler(Looper.getMainLooper(), Callback) with a lambda safe? → A Kotlin lambda capturing this still holds the Activity; a lambda not capturing is safe.
  • Can a Message with no delay leak? → It leaks only for microseconds; the issue is long delays and re-arming loops.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "pull to refresh again in 30 s" feature kept five previous Activities alive on tablets; the symptom was OOM in an unrelated screen, which sent the team profiling image caching for a week before anyone read the retention path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain why a Handler keeps an Activity alive.
  • Hire: draws the root path (MessageQueue -> Message -> Handler -> Activity) and fixes with removeCallbacks or lifecycle-aware scoping.
  • Strong hire: notes re-arming loops, WeakReference is insufficient alone, migrates to repeatOnLifecycle, and adds lint plus CI leak test.

questions.promptHtml: How do you cancel a delayed postDelayed task? Why does handler.removeCallbacks { ... } with a fresh lambda not cancel anything?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A small bug with big consequences (leaked or doubled callbacks); checks that you know matching is by identity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: removeCallbacks(Runnable) removes pending messages whose callback is the same object (reference equality for plain Runnables). A fresh lambda is a new object (or for non-capturing lambdas a different instance than the one you posted via a SAM-converted lambda in a different call site), so nothing matches. Keep the Runnable in a field, or use a token / what, or removeCallbacksAndMessages(null) to clear everything for that Handler.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Handler.removeCallbacks(r) -> mQueue.removeMessages(this, r, null): walks the list and removes messages with p.target == h && p.callback == r.
  • Variants: removeCallbacks(r, token), removeMessages(what), removeMessages(what, obj), removeCallbacksAndMessages(token) where null token means "all messages for this Handler".
  • It removes only pending messages. A message currently executing, or already dispatched, cannot be cancelled; guard with a flag if needed.
  • Removal is O(n) in queue length and takes the queue's monitor, so it is cheap for normal queues but avoid in tight loops with thousands of pending messages (see Q128).
  • Debounce pattern: one stored Runnable, removeCallbacks(task); postDelayed(task, 300).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
private val search = Runnable { runQuery(pendingQuery) }

fun onTextChanged(q: String) {
    pendingQuery = q
    handler.removeCallbacks(search)       // same object -> works
    handler.postDelayed(search, 300)
}

// Broken: a new Runnable each time, nothing to match
fun broken() {
    handler.postDelayed({ doIt() }, 5_000)
    handler.removeCallbacks { doIt() }    // no-op
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating a new lambda in removeCallbacks; silently does nothing.
  • Cancelling in onDestroy only; if the Activity is stopped for minutes, the task fires on a hidden UI. Pair with onStop or lifecycle observers.
  • Assuming it prevents an already-running Runnable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you cancel everything this Handler posted? → removeCallbacksAndMessages(null).
  2. How would you cancel only one feature's messages on a shared Handler? → Post with a token (postAtTime(r, token, time)) and remove by token, or use what codes.
  3. Is there a way to check if a task is pending? → hasMessages(what) and hasCallbacks(runnable) (API 29).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "call removeCallbacks." Senior: knows identity matching, tokens, pending-only semantics, O(n) cost, and that lifecycle-aware coroutines make the whole problem go away.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A debounce that "never debounced" because each keystroke built a new Runnable; the backend saw one request per character.

questions.promptHtml: How does MessageQueue.next() actually work? How does the main thread sleep, wake up for a delayed message, and wake up for input?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat the loop as a black box from those who can reason about idle behavior, wakeups, battery use, and ordering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: next() loops: call nativePollOnce(ptr, timeoutMs), which blocks in epoll_wait on the native Looper; after it returns, look at the head of the time-sorted list. If the head is due, unlink and return it; if it is in the future, compute the remaining time as the next timeout and (if idle handlers exist) run them; if the list is empty, timeout is -1 (sleep until woken). enqueueMessage inserts into the sorted list and, if the new message is at the head (or a barrier case), calls nativeWake to write to an eventfd that wakes the poll. Input and vsync reach the loop through file descriptors registered on the same native Looper, so epoll wakes for them without any Java message.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Java:  Looper.loop() -> MessageQueue.next()
                          |
                          v
Native: Looper::pollOnce(timeoutMillis)  -> epoll_wait on:
          - wake eventfd           (nativeWake from enqueueMessage)
          - InputChannel fd        (touch/key events)
          - DisplayEventReceiver fd(vsync)
          - other fds added by addOnFileDescriptorEventListener (API 23+)

Key steps in next():

  1. nextPollTimeoutMillis = 0 first iteration.
  2. nativePollOnce(ptr, nextPollTimeoutMillis).
  3. Under synchronized(this): read mMessages. If the head has target == null it is a sync barrier (see Q119): scan forward for the first asynchronous message.
  4. If msg.when > now: nextPollTimeoutMillis = min(msg.when - now, Integer.MAX_VALUE). Else unlink, mark in use, return.
  5. If no message: timeout = -1; run IdleHandlers (once per next() call) before sleeping; if any returns false, remove it.
  6. If mQuitting, dispose() and return null.

enqueueMessage inserts by when, keeping stability for equal when. needWake is true when the new message becomes the head (or for async messages when there is a barrier and it is the first async one). Cost: insertion O(n) in pending messages; dispatch O(1). Everything is guarded by one monitor, so producers on many threads contend on it, but critical sections are tiny.

Why no battery drain at idle: with an empty queue, timeout is -1 and the thread sleeps in the kernel; the CPU can enter low power. A timed wake is only as precise as the kernel timer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Observing what is pending (debug only; the dump is for diagnostics, not production logic)
Looper.getMainLooper().dump(android.util.LogPrinter(Log.DEBUG, "LOOPER"), "")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "the loop polls every N ms". It sleeps until woken by a precise event or timeout.
  • Believing delayed messages are in a separate structure; they share the same sorted list.
  • Assuming input events are Messages. They come over the input channel fd and are turned into callbacks inside ViewRootImpl's receiver, and they are not subject to your postDelayed ordering the same way.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can heavy postAtFrontOfQueue starve the queue? → Messages with when = 0 are inserted at the head, ahead of everything due.
  2. What wakes a sleeping main thread when a worker posts a message? → nativeWake writes to the eventfd the epoll watches.
  3. What happens to messages if the queue is quit? → quit() removes all (or only future ones for quitSafely), and later enqueues return false.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "a queue with a loop." Senior: sorted linked list, epoll/eventfd, fd-based input and vsync, idle handler placement, barriers, and O(n) insertion consequences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A trace showed "main thread sleeping" yet the UI was frozen: a leaked sync barrier was making next() skip every normal message while still sleeping happily.

questions.promptHtml: What are sync barriers and asynchronous messages in MessageQueue? Who uses them and what breaks if a barrier is leaked?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Deep platform knowledge; explains how frames get priority over ordinary posts and a rare but nasty class of "app is alive but nothing happens" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A sync barrier is a special message with target == null placed in the queue; while it is at the head, next() skips all synchronous messages and delivers only messages marked asynchronous, until someone removes the barrier by its token. ViewRootImpl posts a barrier when it schedules a traversal so that vsync/Choreographer frame messages (async) run ahead of ordinary posts, and removes it when the traversal runs. A leaked barrier means every normal Handler.post, including lifecycle H messages, stops being delivered, while async frame messages and input still work, so the app looks half-alive and eventually ANRs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• MessageQueue.postSyncBarrier() is @hide; it returns an int token (token-based since API 23). removeSyncBarrier(token) removes it. Apps cannot call these without reflection/hidden API access; do not.
  • Async messages: Message.setAsynchronous(true), or a Handler made with Handler.createAsync(looper) (API 28; HandlerCompat.createAsync for older). Async messages are ordered among themselves by when; barrier only affects whether sync messages may pass.
  • Framework use: ViewRootImpl.scheduleTraversals() -> mTraversalBarrier = mHandler.getLooper().getQueue().postSyncBarrier() then mChoreographer.postCallback(TRAVERSAL, ...). doTraversal() calls removeSyncBarrier(mTraversalBarrier). Choreographer's own frame messages are setAsynchronous(true).
  • Result: when a frame is pending, ordinary posts cannot cut in front of the traversal that was requested.
  • Leak symptom: touch still lights ripples (input fd path) and animations may run, but handler.post {}, runOnUiThread, view.post, lifecycle changes and broadcasts never execute. ANR traces show the main thread idle in nativePollOnce with a non-empty queue.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.Build
import android.os.Handler
import android.os.Looper

fun asyncHandler(): Handler =
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 28) Handler.createAsync(Looper.getMainLooper())
    else Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())   // or HandlerCompat.createAsync(Looper.getMainLooper())
// Use sparingly: async messages bypass barriers, so they can jump ahead of traversals' sync work.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Marking everything async for "priority"; it competes with frame work and does not make code faster.
  • Using hidden postSyncBarrier via reflection; blocked/greylisted on newer APIs and dangerous if you forget removal.
  • Confusing barriers with postAtFrontOfQueue; a barrier changes eligibility, not position.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Choreographer need async messages? → So the frame callbacks run even while a traversal barrier is up.
  2. How would you detect a leaked barrier in a trace? → Perfetto shows main thread sleeping while ANR dumps show messages with when in the past still queued, usually after a hung traversal.
  3. Do Handler.post ordering guarantees still hold with async handlers? → Only among messages of the same kind; sync and async messages can reorder relative to each other whenever a barrier is present.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "never heard of it." Senior: explains target == null, who posts barriers, token API, async messages, and the symptom signature of a leak.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A third-party tweak library that reflected into postSyncBarrier crashed mid-call and never removed the barrier, producing "tap works but nothing updates" reports on one OEM's builds.

questions.promptHtml: What is a MessageQueue.IdleHandler? When is it called and what are the rules for using it safely?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of a niche but useful hook used for deferring non-critical startup work and by the framework itself; also checks understanding of "idle".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An IdleHandler runs when the queue has nothing due to run right now: the head message is in the future or the queue is empty. queueIdle() returns true to stay registered for future idle moments, false to be removed after this call. It runs on the Looper's thread, so it blocks messages that arrive while it runs. It is good for small deferrable work (warming a cache after first frame) but not a place for heavy work, and it provides no deadline guarantee.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Register: Looper.myQueue().addIdleHandler(handler) (call on the target thread) or looper.queue.addIdleHandler on API 23+.
  • In next(): when no message is due and pendingIdleHandlerCount < 0, it snapshots the registered handlers (max once per next() call, i.e. once per idle period) and calls queueIdle() outside the lock. Then the loop re-checks the queue because the idle handler may have posted work.
  • "Idle" is per-queue: between frames the main queue is often idle, so IdleHandlers can run between frames. A handler that does 20 ms of work will cause a jank frame, exactly like any message.
  • Starvation: on a busy main thread (animations, constant posting) idle moments are rare, so the work could be delayed for a long time. No timeout.
  • Framework uses: ActivityThread registers GC idler and Idler (reports activityIdle to AMS after first resume); ViewRootImpl uses idle wiring for some drawing hints. Use these as evidence, not recipe.
  • Jetpack alternatives: Choreographer postFrameCallback for "after first frame", reportFullyDrawn() for measurement, App Startup/coroutines with Dispatchers.Default for background init.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.Looper
import android.os.MessageQueue

fun warmUpWhenIdle() {
    Looper.myQueue().addIdleHandler(object : MessageQueue.IdleHandler {
        override fun queueIdle(): Boolean {
            prefetchSmallTables()   // keep this tiny (< 2-3 ms)
            return false            // run once, then unregister
        }
    })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning true by accident: runs on every idle period forever, burning frames.
  • Heavy work inside queueIdle() causing jank because "idle" does not mean "free".
  • Registering from a thread without a Looper (Looper.myQueue() null/throws) or registering many handlers that capture Activities (leak until they return false).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is it different from handler.postDelayed(r, 100)? → Delay is time-based and runs regardless of load; idle is state-based and can be starved or run immediately.
  2. Can you use it to wait for first frame? → Not reliably; use Choreographer.postFrameCallback / doOnPreDraw / reportFullyDrawn.
  3. Who removes it? → You, by returning false or calling removeIdleHandler.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "runs when main thread is idle, good for startup work." Senior: knows it only runs when no message is due, still runs on the main thread, can be starved, and that background threads are usually the correct tool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved SDK init to an IdleHandler to speed up startup, but on feed-heavy screens idle moments never came, so analytics events were dropped for the first minute.

questions.contextHtml: A medication-reminder app (600k DAU) lets users start a "take pill in 20 minutes" countdown. The implementation: handler.postDelayed({ showReminderNotification() }, 20 * 60_000) from a foreground Activity, then the user locks the phone. Support tickets: "reminder came at 47 minutes", worst on Android 12-14 Pixels and Samsung; none on the QA phone that sits on a charger with the screen on. Telemetry shows fired_at - scheduled_at p50 = 21 min, p95 = 58 min, max = 6 h. There is a red herring: the app also has an FCM data message for server-side reminders that arrives on time.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the local reminder late, and how do you make it reliable?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Doze is killing the Handler; use a foreground service." A foreground service for a one-off reminder is heavy-handed and may need a type/permission; they also cannot explain why the delay is variable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the countdown user-visible after the screen turns off (does exactness matter to the minute)? Is the app process still alive when it fires, or killed? Is the device charging? Is an exact alarm acceptable policy-wise (calendar/alarm-clock-like use)? What targetSdk?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the schedule to AlarmManager: setAlarmClock or setExactAndAllowWhileIdle (needs SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM/USE_EXACT_ALARM conditions; B1 chunk), keep the Handler only for the in-app visual countdown. Keep the server FCM reminder as a backup channel.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Handler clock is uptime-based; when the screen is off the CPU can enter suspend, so the 20-minute delay counts only awake time; (b) the process is cached/frozen or killed, so the callback never runs; (c) Doze/standby deferring network, not the Handler itself; (d) bug in app logic. Red herring: FCM is a high-priority path, so it is not comparable.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log both uptimeMillis and elapsedRealtime at schedule/fire; the gap between them is time spent in deep sleep (here about 26 min). adb shell dumpsys deviceidle and dumpsys alarm to see Doze state and registered alarms; adb shell dumpsys battery unplug + adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle to reproduce; Perfetto power track to see suspend intervals.
  5. Root cause: postDelayed schedules at uptimeMillis() + delay. uptimeMillis does not advance while the CPU is suspended. With the screen off and no wake lock the kernel suspends; time on the "Handler clock" stops. The Looper wakes only when something else (alarm, push, user) wakes the CPU, then catches up late. That also means the callback is not guaranteed to run at all if the process was killed or frozen meanwhile.
  6. Fix: Short term: AlarmManager setExactAndAllowWhileIdle with a PendingIntent to a receiver that posts the notification (works from a cold process). Long term: persist the target as an absolute wall-clock time in Room/DataStore, re-register alarms on BOOT_COMPLETED, TIMEZONE_CHANGED/TIME_SET, and package replacement, and use elapsedRealtime-based alarm type for timers, RTC_WAKEUP for clock times. Verify the exact-alarm permission flow (API 31+/33/34 rules) on developer.android.com.
  7. Prevention: A device-farm test with screen-off for 30 minutes; telemetry for lateness; a code-review rule: "a Handler delay is never a wall-clock promise".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not hold a partial wake lock for 20 minutes (battery, Play vitals "stuck partial wake lock" flagged). I would not default to a foreground service just to keep a Handler alive. I'd also not use WorkManager for a minute-accurate user timer: it is for deferrable work and has no timing guarantee.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user force-stops the app? → Alarms are cleared on force stop; the app will not fire until the user launches it again. Document it; nothing more can be done.
  • What if exactness only matters at +-10 min? → setAndAllowWhileIdle (inexact) is fine and avoids the exact alarm permission.
  • On Android 14, exact alarm permission is denied by default for newer installs targeting 33+; what do you do? → Check canScheduleExactAlarms(), route to the special-access settings screen, or use USE_EXACT_ALARM if the app qualifies as alarm/timer/calendar; fallback to inexact otherwise.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A habit-tracker "focus timer" shipped on Handlers; it passed all internal tests (devs hold their phones) and failed in the wild because test phones never sat idle in a pocket for 25 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames "Android killing the app" without identifying the clock.
  • Hire: identifies uptime vs elapsed, proposes AlarmManager with correct API.
  • Strong hire: instruments both clocks to prove it, handles reboot/time change/exact alarm policy, and rejects wake locks and unneeded FGS.

questions.promptHtml: How does Choreographer relate to the Looper and MessageQueue? Walk through what happens between invalidate() and pixels, at the message level.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Links the Looper model to rendering; the foundation for jank analysis. (Frame deadlines and input dispatch details are covered in M2; here the interviewer wants the queue-level mechanics.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Choreographer is a per-thread singleton (created lazily for a thread with a Looper) that sequences work to display vsync. invalidate() or requestLayout() leads to ViewRootImpl.scheduleTraversals(), which posts a sync barrier and asks Choreographer for a TRAVERSAL callback. Choreographer requests the next vsync from the display event receiver; when vsync arrives (as a file descriptor event on the Looper), it enqueues an asynchronous message that runs doFrame, which runs callbacks in order INPUT, ANIMATION, INSETS_ANIMATION, TRAVERSAL, COMMIT. The traversal removes the barrier, measures, lays out and draws (recording display lists; RenderThread does the GPU part).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
invalidate()
  -> ViewRootImpl.scheduleTraversals()
        postSyncBarrier()                     (blocks ordinary posts)
        Choreographer.postCallback(TRAVERSAL)
           -> scheduleFrameLocked -> request vsync (DisplayEventReceiver)
vsync arrives (fd event on the Looper thread)
  -> async Message(MSG_DO_FRAME)  -> Choreographer.doFrame(frameTimeNanos)
        INPUT callbacks (batched touch events)
        ANIMATION callbacks (ValueAnimator, postFrameCallback)
        TRAVERSAL callback -> doTraversal(): removeSyncBarrier -> performMeasure/Layout/Draw
        COMMIT callbacks
  • frameTimeNanos is the vsync timestamp the frame is "about", not "now"; skipped frames are detected by now - frameTimeNanos > one frame interval, logging "Skipped N frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread" when N >= 30 (it logs at 30+ frames by default).
  • Choreographer posts its own messages to a FrameHandler bound to the thread's Looper and marks them asynchronous so the barrier does not block them.
  • Choreographer.getInstance().postFrameCallback(cb) runs cb.doFrame(frameTimeNanos) once on the next frame (re-post to continue), i.e. in the ANIMATION group. API 33 added postVsyncCallback with frame-timeline data; check the docs before relying on it.
  • Because frame work is a single message on the main Looper, anything that runs before it in the same vsync window (a 30 ms onClick) delays the frame: the "missed vsync".
  • One Choreographer per Looper thread; a SurfaceView/render thread can have its own with its own Looper.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.view.Choreographer

class FrameMeter : Choreographer.FrameCallback {
    private var last = 0L
    fun start() = Choreographer.getInstance().postFrameCallback(this)
    override fun doFrame(frameTimeNanos: Long) {
        if (last != 0L) {
            val ms = (frameTimeNanos - last) / 1_000_000.0
            if (ms > 20) android.util.Log.w("Frame", "slow frame interval $ms ms")
        }
        last = frameTimeNanos
        Choreographer.getInstance().postFrameCallback(this)   // re-arm
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to re-post in doFrame (callbacks are one-shot) or to remove callbacks (removeFrameCallback), leaking and keeping the screen "dirty".
  • Treating doFrame time as the start of work; use the supplied timestamp for animation math, not System.nanoTime().
  • Thinking Choreographer is a thread; it is a sequencer on the existing Looper.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the traversal "protected" by a barrier? → So ordinary posts cannot be inserted between the invalidate and the frame, avoiding extra delay (and later reordering).
  2. What happens on a 120 Hz display? → vsync period 8.33 ms; the same machinery but half the budget; adaptive refresh may choose lower rates.
  3. Where does RenderThread fit? → After the main-thread draw, the record is handed to RenderThread, which issues GPU work; main thread jank and RenderThread jank are different in traces.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Choreographer syncs with vsync." Senior: knows the barrier plus async-message trick, callback group order, the frameTime semantics, and where main vs render work separates in Perfetto.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom animation loop based on Handler.postDelayed(16) stuttered; replacing it with postFrameCallback and frameTimeNanos removed uneven steps.

questions.promptHtml: How is Dispatchers.Main implemented on Android? What is the difference between Dispatchers.Main and Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and how does delay work there?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand that coroutines on Android are not magic but ride the same Looper, and the ordering and reentrancy consequences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The kotlinx-coroutines-android artifact provides a main dispatcher backed by a Handler on the main Looper (a HandlerContext; on API 28+ it uses an async Handler). dispatch() simply posts the continuation as a Runnable. Dispatchers.Main.immediate skips the post if you are already on the main thread, running the block inline; Dispatchers.Main always posts. delay on that dispatcher is implemented with handler.postDelayed, and cancellation removes the callback. So all the Looper rules apply: uptime-based delays, one message at a time, ordering by posting time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Registration: AndroidDispatcherFactory creates HandlerContext(Looper.getMainLooper().asHandler(async = true)). Async handlers' messages are not blocked by sync barriers (consequence: they can run while a traversal is pending, which is generally desired for responsiveness).
  • isDispatchNeeded(context): for immediate returns Looper.myLooper() != handler.looper; for plain Main returns true.
  • Ordering consequence: with Main, launch { A } always runs after the current message completes, so code after launch runs first. With Main.immediate, launch { A } runs A synchronously up to its first suspension, so A runs before the code after launch. lifecycleScope and viewModelScope use Dispatchers.Main.immediate.
  • delay(n): HandlerContext implements Delay: scheduleResumeAfterDelay posts a Runnable with postDelayed(n); on cancel it calls removeCallbacks. Therefore it inherits the uptime behavior (Q113) and does not tick in deep sleep.
  • Not every suspension hops: resuming a continuation after withContext(Dispatchers.IO) posts back to the main Handler via dispatch; resuming in Main.immediate from the main thread executes via an event loop to avoid deep stacks (unconfined-style nested loop guard).
  • Testing: Dispatchers.setMain(...) with StandardTestDispatcher; the Looper-based dispatcher is replaced.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import kotlinx.coroutines.*

fun demo(scope: CoroutineScope) {   // scope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate
    scope.launch {
        println("A")                         // prints before C if immediate
        delay(1)
        println("B")
    }
    println("C")
}
// Dispatchers.Main:           C A B
// Dispatchers.Main.immediate: A C B  (A runs inline until the first suspension, then C)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Dispatchers.Main and .immediate are interchangeable in tests/ordering-sensitive code.
  • Using Thread.sleep in a coroutine on Main; blocks the Looper like any other call.
  • Expecting delay(10 min) to be wall-time accurate in the background.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does launch(Dispatchers.Main) inside onCreate not update UI before onCreate returns? → It posts; the continuation runs after the current lifecycle message.
  2. What is Dispatchers.Main.immediate's risk? → Reentrancy: code you call inline may mutate state you are in the middle of changing; use Main if you need strict deferral.
  3. How does cancellation propagate to a pending delay? → Removes the posted callback via the Handler.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Main is the UI thread dispatcher." Senior: knows HandlerContext, async Handler, immediate's inline execution and its ordering consequences, and that delay is postDelayed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics event fired "before" a screen's state was set because a team switched a scope from Main.immediate to Main, changing ordering of two coroutines.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (3M DAU) sees ANR rate rise from 0.3% to 1.1% after a release (Play Console threshold for "bad behavior" is 0.47% user-perceived ANR). Android Vitals clusters show the main thread idle or inside generic framework frames:

"main" tid=1 Native
  at android.os.MessageQueue.nativePollOnce(Native method)
  at android.os.Looper.loop(Looper.java:299)
  at android.app.ActivityThread.main(ActivityThread.java:8282)
Reason: Input dispatching timed out (... Waiting to send non-key event because the touched window has not finished processing certain input events that were delivered to it over 500.0ms ago.)

Other traces (only 20%) show SharedPreferences.apply -> QueuedWork.waitToFinish and a few show a JSON parse. The release added 14 PRs, three touching background sync.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find which message is stalling the main Looper when stack traces are inconclusive, and what do you do in the first 24 hours?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Look at the stack trace and fix what's on top." The sampled main-thread stack was captured at the ANR moment, not at the time of the slow message; the stall may have ended by then or the head of the queue is blocking something else.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the rate release-correlated (versions) or device/OS-correlated? Which ANR types dominate (input vs broadcast vs service)? Are traces mostly idle (stall already ended) or in blocking calls? What changed in sync (do we post many main-thread messages)? Are we sampling slow messages today?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout and compare cohorts; if a feature flag exists for the new sync logic, turn it off for 50%; keep the rollback ready.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A burst of main-thread posts from a new sync (hundreds of small messages each doing work) starving input/frames; (b) one long message (SharedPreferences apply waits in QueuedWork during onStop/onPause, JSON on main); (c) binder call to a slow system service from main (see X chunk); (d) lock contention with a background thread holding a monitor. Idle-looking traces fit (a) and "stall ended" patterns.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a debug/staged-rollout Looper.getMainLooper().setMessageLogging(printer) that parses ">>>>> Dispatching to Handler (cls) {hash} callback: what" and "<<<<< Finished to" lines, timing each pair and logging the Handler class plus callback class when over 100 ms; sample on 1% of sessions. Perfetto with sched, binder_driver, and atrace categories (view, am, wm) to see message slices and who holds the CPU; Android Studio CPU profiler "system trace". Check StrictMode logs for disk/network on main.
  5. Root cause (in this scenario): the new sync wrote 400 rows via Dispatchers.Main callbacks, one main.post per row, each doing a 3-8 ms Room-less in-memory merge and notifying LiveData; a burst of 400 x 5 ms = 2 s of queued work. Touches arriving during the burst waited behind them. The input dispatcher expects the window to acknowledge each event within 5 s; the "Waiting to send ... over 500ms ago" text just says events are queued behind unacknowledged ones. Several overlapping bursts (each sync triggered 2-3 times by retries) pushed the oldest unacknowledged event past 5 s. (Exact message wording varies by release.)
  6. Fix: Short term: batch the updates into one message and apply a single diff to the adapter; move the merge to Dispatchers.Default; throttle with conflate. Long term: a SlowMessageDetector in production tooling, and Choreographer-aware work chunking (yield() or break into 4 ms slices).
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark / frame timing in CI; Vitals dashboards by version; StrictMode detectAll in debug; a lint rule against main.post in loops; budget for main-thread time per feature.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't ship a raw Printer-based logger to 100% of users: it allocates a string per message (two per dispatched message) and adds measurable overhead; sample or use a lighter hook (e.g. a FrameMetrics listener or ApplicationExitInfo for ANR traces). I wouldn't "increase timeouts" (not controllable) or add try/catch around everything.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does ApplicationExitInfo help? → Yes (API 30+): REASON_ANR with traceInputStream gives the system's own ANR trace for the previous session; upload on next start.
  • Why would the trace be idle in nativePollOnce? → The slow message finished before the dump was taken; the ANR came from the input dispatcher timing, not from the current stack.
  • Could this be caused by another process? → Yes: CPU starvation from other processes shows as long runnable states in Perfetto; check sched data before blaming the code.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A broadcast storm of 2,000 per-item notifies after a bulk sync looked like "random ANRs"; a 1% sampled message logger pointed at one Handler class within a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: relies on the ANR stack alone.
  • Hire: proposes Looper message logging or Perfetto to find slow messages, and batches work.
  • Strong hire: understands sampling vs overhead, uses ApplicationExitInfo, distinguishes input-dispatch ANR from stack-at-dump, and sets prevention budgets.

questions.contextHtml: A messaging app with 5M DAU has a 7-year-old MessageSyncer built on Handler plus callbacks. You are asked to migrate it to coroutines in two sprints without a feature freeze. The class's contract is undocumented, but tests show it relies on: (1) results delivered on the main thread in the order requests were made; (2) a postDelayed retry with backoff 2 s/4 s/8 s; (3) a cancel path on Activity destroy that calls removeCallbacksAndMessages(null). A previous migration attempt caused duplicated messages for 0.3% of users.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate safely, and what behavior might silently change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace Handler with launch and delay, done." Ignores ordering, cancellation, exceptions and wall-time semantics; a big-bang switch under live traffic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which callers rely on ordering? Is the work idempotent? What is the cancellation scope today (Activity vs process)? What is the crash baseline and the rollout mechanism (remote config)? Is delay timing precision important?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is planned work. Immediate step: characterisation tests documenting current behavior (ordering, retry timings, cancel) before touching code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) Ordering: Handler.post guarantees FIFO for equal when, but launch on Dispatchers.Default/IO does not; (b) cancellation semantics: removeCallbacksAndMessages stops pending but not running work; coroutine cancellation is cooperative and also cancels finally-less work; (c) exceptions: Handler crashes the process; a launch without handler propagates to the scope (viewModelScope crashes if uncaught too, but supervisorScope/CoroutineExceptionHandler change the failure mode); (d) scope lifetime: moving to lifecycleScope cancels on destroy but process-wide syncs may need an application scope; (e) delay is uptime based too, same as postDelayed, so no regression, but also no improvement.
  4. How I'd verify each: Characterisation tests with a fake Looper (Robolectric shadowOf(looper) idle) and runTest with virtual time; stress test with 1,000 rapid requests and assert order; staged rollout via flag at 1%/10%/50% comparing duplicate-message rate and crash-free sessions in dashboards.
  5. Root cause of the earlier incident: the old code serialized through a single Looper; the new code ran two coroutines concurrently and both retried the same message because there was no single-writer guard.
  6. Fix (plan): Keep a single-consumer boundary: expose suspend fun send() that pushes into a Channel consumed by one coroutine (serial), keep results delivered on Dispatchers.Main; implement retries with delay inside that consumer; provide cancel() via scope cancellation; keep both implementations behind a flag, shadow-run compare in debug builds; remove Handler only after two releases.
  7. Prevention: Idempotency keys on message sends; metrics on duplicates; detekt/lint to forbid new Handler use in this module.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't rewrite the whole syncer at once or swap threading and logic together. I wouldn't use GlobalScope for convenience (no cancellation). I wouldn't use Dispatchers.Main.immediate in the consumer without reviewing reentrancy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The old code ran retries via postDelayed and survived configuration changes because the Handler lived in a singleton. What replaces that? → An application-scoped coroutine scope (or WorkManager if it must survive process death), not the Activity scope.
  • A test shows ordering differs under load. Why? → Multiple launch calls on a multi-thread dispatcher; fix by single consumer or limitedParallelism(1).
  • Is HandlerThread.asCoroutineDispatcher() a fair intermediate step? → Yes; handler.asCoroutineDispatcher() preserves the single-thread ordering while you convert call sites.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "mechanical" migration doubled push notifications for 0.4% of users because retry coroutines were launched per request instead of per queue; the fix was a single-consumer channel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: direct replacement with no ordering or cancel analysis.
  • Hire: lists ordering, cancellation, exception and scope differences, and uses a flag.
  • Strong hire: single-writer design, characterisation tests, shadow runs, staged rollout metrics and clear rollback.

questions.contextHtml:
A document-scanner app (1.2M DAU) crashed for 0.9% of sessions on 3 GB devices after a release, always after the user had scanned many pages. Crashlytics:

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Try again
    at java.lang.Thread.nativeCreate(Native Method)
    at java.lang.Thread.start(Thread.java:1063)
    at android.os.HandlerThread.start(...)
    at com.app.scan.PageProcessor.<init>(PageProcessor.kt:18)

PageProcessor is created per scanned page; its init does HandlerThread("page-proc").apply { start() }. No quit anywhere. Thread count in adb shell ls /proc/<pid>/task | wc -l is 1,400 on a crashing device. The heap is fine (red herring: the team first raised largeHeap). A previous postmortem blamed "Android memory".
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: what happened, why it was invisible, and what changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap / use a thread pool." Misses that this OOM is about native thread limits, and does not explain why a HandlerThread never ends by itself.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What do the thread counts look like over a session (per-page growth)? Does OOM correlate with device RAM or with ulimit/thread limit? Does PageProcessor hold references (bitmaps, Activity)? When did the creation pattern change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: share one process-wide HandlerThread (or a single-thread dispatcher) and make PageProcessor use its Handler; ship via a staged rollout. Stop the bleeding without redesign.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Threads leak: each HandlerThread parks in Looper.loop() forever; (b) native stack allocation (1 MB virtual each plus kernel limits per process such as max_user_processes/thread limits) exhausted, not Java heap; (c) leaks of what the threads reference (each thread's Handler may capture a page bitmap).
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell ls /proc/<pid>/task | wc -l before/after scanning pages; adb shell cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep Threads; thread dump (kill -3 or Android Studio) showing hundreds of "page-proc" threads in nativePollOnce; compare dumpsys meminfo Java heap (stable) vs native/stack.
  5. Root cause: A Looper thread does not exit until quit() is called. HandlerThread is not tied to any lifecycle; it is not GC'd while running because a live thread is a GC root. Each page created one, so N pages = N parked threads, each reserving a stack and kernel structures, until pthread_create failed. The per-process thread ceiling is device-dependent, which is why only some devices crashed.
  6. Fix: Short-term: single shared processor thread. Long-term: replace per-instance threads with one CoroutineDispatcher (Dispatchers.Default, or Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) for serial work), owned by a lifecycle-aware class; if a Looper is genuinely needed, create it lazily and quitSafely() in close(), with Closeable use enforced.
  7. Prevention: A StrictMode-like debug check: log thread count after each major flow; an instrumented test asserting thread count is stable over 100 iterations; lint/Detekt for HandlerThread( outside a shared provider; track Threads: from /proc/self/status as a custom metric.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't raise largeHeap (wrong resource). I wouldn't rely on finalizers or WeakReference to kill threads. I'd not make the shared thread quit on every screen exit; stopping and starting thrashes and races queued work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the owner is destroyed while a message is running? → quitSafely() lets due messages finish; design the Runnables to check a cancelled flag; avoid join() on the main thread.
  • Does a Kotlin Executors.newFixedThreadPool leak the same way? → Yes, unless shutdown(); pool threads are non-daemon by default.
  • Why no OOM in the Java heap graph? → The cost is native memory and thread-count limits, which a heap dump does not show.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "tiny helper class" used in a list adapter created a HandlerThread per ViewHolder bind; thread count grew with scroll distance and the crash was reported as "random OOM on scroll".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: attributes it to heap size and proposes largeHeap.
  • Hire: identifies leaked looper threads and fixes with a shared thread/quit.
  • Strong hire: measures thread counts, explains native stack/thread limits, adds a metric and tests, and writes blameless prevention items.

questions.subtopic: Quitting Loopers, exceptions in the loop
questions.promptHtml: What happens when you call quit() on a Looper, when you post to a quit Looper, when you try to quit the main Looper, and when a Runnable throws inside the loop?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Edge behavior that decides whether shutdown is clean, whether work is silently lost, and why exceptions in handlers crash the app.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: quit() marks the queue as quitting, drops all pending messages, and makes next() return null so loop() returns and the thread can end; quitSafely() drops only future-dated messages and lets due ones run. Posting afterwards returns false, recycles the message, and logs "sending message to a Handler on a dead thread". The main Looper cannot be quit: it throws IllegalStateException("Main thread not allowed to quit."). An uncaught exception in a Runnable propagates out of Looper.loop(), up the thread, and on the main thread the default handler terminates the process (the stack shows Handler.dispatchMessage and Looper.loop).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• MessageQueue.quit(safe): sets mQuitting, calls removeAllFutureMessagesLocked() (safe) or removeAllMessagesLocked() (unsafe), then nativeWake.
  • enqueueMessage when mQuitting: msg.recycle(); return false. Callers that ignore the boolean silently lose work.
  • Main Looper is created with quitAllowed = false; prepare(false) marks it. Background loopers from prepare() allow quit.
  • Exceptions: Looper.loop() does not catch exceptions thrown by dispatchMessage. On the main thread they hit RuntimeInit's uncaught handler: crash. On a HandlerThread the thread dies too (and the default uncaught handler kills the process, because Android installs one for all threads in the app process). So one bad Runnable on any thread with the app's default handler crashes the app, not just that thread.
  • Catching: wrap the body of risky Runnables in try/catch, or install a Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler on the HandlerThread only for logging; do not swallow crashes globally (state corruption).
  • A dead looper thread's Handler remains usable as an object but all posts fail.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val ok = handler.post { work() }
if (!ok) {
    // Looper is quitting; decide: drop, retry elsewhere, or log metrics
    Log.w("Q", "post rejected: looper quitting")
}

// Safe shutdown
thread.quitSafely()

// Throws IllegalStateException: Main thread not allowed to quit.
// Looper.getMainLooper().quit()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring post() return value on a Looper that may be quitting.
