  • Assuming an exception in a HandlerThread only kills that thread.
  • Assuming quitSafely runs messages posted with a delay; it does not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if you call quit() from inside a message on that Looper? → Allowed; the current message finishes, then the loop ends.
  2. Can you restart a quit Looper? → No; create a new thread/Looper.
  3. How do crash reporters see Handler exceptions? → Through the default uncaught handler, same as any thread; the stack's root frames show the Handler path.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "quit stops the thread." Senior: differentiates quit vs quitSafely, return value of post, main not quittable, and that the app-wide uncaught handler turns a worker exception into a process crash.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Telemetry events vanished at app close because the logging HandlerThread was quit() (not quitSafely()) in onTerminate-like cleanup and dropped the last batch.

questions.contextHtml: A chat app supports disappearing messages. Each message item posts its own expiry: handler.postDelayed(expiryRunnable(id), ttl); scrolling cancels with handler.removeCallbacks(runnable) when a row is unbound. Today a typical power user has ~500 pending expiries. A new "Communities" feature will load up to 5,000 messages per screen and 30 rows get bound/unbound per scroll frame. Prototype numbers on a mid-range device: scroll p95 frame time 9 ms today, 31 ms in the prototype; Perfetto shows main-thread slices in MessageQueue.enqueueMessage and removeMessages growing; no GC pressure issues. A teammate says "postDelayed is cheap, it's a timer."
questions.promptHtml: Why does this degrade at 10x, and how would you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WorkManager" or "reduce delays". Wrong tool, and doesn't explain cost of the data structure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the expiries need to fire while the screen is visible or also in background (affects the mechanism)? How accurate must expiry be (1 s vs 1 min)? Is the expiry state persisted (database timestamp) or only in memory? Are rows recycled with RecyclerView?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Only register timers for visible rows; unregister on onViewRecycled. That caps pending messages to ~30-50 instead of 5,000.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) MessageQueue is a time-sorted linked list: enqueueMessage is O(n) insertion and removeMessages is O(n) scan, both under the queue monitor, so 30 binds x 5,000 pending nodes per frame is ~150k node visits plus lock contention; (b) allocation churn from lambdas/Runnables; (c) the expiry logic itself is slow; (d) diffing in the adapter (red herring, flat in Perfetto).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto/system trace showing time inside enqueueMessage/removeMessages; microbenchmark inserting/removing 5,000 messages; a counter for pending messages per Looper (debug dump()); Macrobenchmark scroll test before/after.
  5. Root cause: Using the Looper as a general-purpose timer wheel for thousands of independent timers. The structure is built for a handful of pending messages; each operation scales with queue size and the monitor is shared with everyone else who posts, including Choreographer.
  6. Fix: Short term: visible-rows-only timers. Long term: one scheduler object with a PriorityQueue (or sorted map) of expiryTime -> id, plus exactly one pending Handler message for the earliest deadline (reschedule on change). On fire, pop all due items in a batch and notify once with a diff. Source of truth: an expiresAt column in the database (System.currentTimeMillis()), so expiry survives process death; use an elapsed/AlarmManager path only if background expiry is required.
  7. Prevention: Microbenchmark in CI for scheduler operations; budget "pending messages per Looper < ~100" as an engineering rule; code review: never post a message per list item.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't move all timers to a background HandlerThread; it hides main-thread cost but keeps the O(n) structure and adds thread-hops for UI updates. I wouldn't use one ScheduledExecutorService task per item (same scale problem, extra threads).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if expiry must fire within 1 s while the app is open but may lag when backgrounded? → One 1 s tick (or earliest-deadline message) plus recompute on resume from expiresAt.
  • Does RecyclerView binding order matter? → Yes; register in onViewAttachedToWindow, unregister in onViewDetachedFromWindow/onViewRecycled, since bind can happen without visibility.
  • Why not Choreographer callbacks? → That ties timers to frames and wakes the display pipeline needlessly; expiries are second-granularity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A countdown-per-row feature scaled fine in the demo (20 rows) and jank appeared only for accounts with thousands of items; a single earliest-deadline scheduler cut queue operations to nearly zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes postDelayed is O(1) and moves on.
  • Hire: identifies O(n) queue operations and limits timers to visible rows or a single scheduler.
  • Strong hire: single earliest-deadline design, persists wall-clock expiry, handles background and process death separately, and benchmarks.

questions.promptHtml: Why do people say "use Message.obtain() instead of new Message()"? How does the Message pool work and what are its failure modes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of allocation behavior in a hot path and of Message reuse rules (recycled objects, "already in use" crashes).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Messages are recycled through a small global linked-list pool (max 50). Message.obtain() takes one from the pool, or allocates if empty; after dispatch the Looper calls recycleUnchecked(), clearing fields and returning it to the pool. This avoids allocation churn for the framework's constant message traffic. You must not touch a Message after sending it, and must not enqueue the same Message twice.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pool: static sPool head, sPoolSize, MAX_POOL_SIZE = 50, guarded by sPoolSync.
  • obtain() unlinks head; clears FLAG_IN_USE. Handler.obtainMessage(...) calls Message.obtain(this, what, ...) and sets the target for you. post(Runnable) obtains internally (via getPostMessage).
  • After dispatch, Looper.loop() calls msg.recycleUnchecked(): sets FLAG_IN_USE, clears what, arg1, arg2, obj, replyTo, data, callback, target, when, and pushes it to the pool if sPoolSize < MAX_POOL_SIZE.
  • Enqueue check: msg.isInUse() -> IllegalStateException("This message is already in use."). Reusing a Message you already sent (e.g. keeping a field and re-sending it) throws, or worse, aliases state after recycling. Use Message.obtain(msg) to copy.
  • msg.recycle() public: throws if it is in use (This message is still in use.); you normally never call it.
  • Cancelled messages (removeMessages) are recycled by the queue.
  • Consequences: do not hold references to a dispatched Message (e.g. to inspect obj later); copy the data in handleMessage.
  • Effect size: the pool is only worth it for high-rate paths; for ordinary code Handler.post already does this and a lambda allocation is usually the bigger cost.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val m = handler.obtainMessage(MSG_DATA, payload)   // pooled, target set
m.sendToTarget()

// Broken: reusing a sent message
val cached = Message.obtain().apply { what = 1 }
handler.sendMessage(cached)
handler.sendMessage(cached)   // IllegalStateException: This message is already in use.

// Correct
handler.sendMessage(Message.obtain(cached))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Holding a Message in a field after sending it; its fields are cleared when recycled.
  • Calling new Message() in hot paths (allocation churn), though it is not incorrect.
  • Assuming the pool is unbounded; beyond 50 free ones, extras are garbage.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the pool thread safe? → Yes, guarded by a lock; it is global across all Looper threads.
  2. What is Message.setData(Bundle) cost? → Allocates a Bundle; arg1/arg2/obj are cheaper.
  3. Are Messages Parcelable for Messenger? → Yes, with restrictions on obj (only Parcelable framework objects across processes).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "obtain avoids garbage." Senior: knows max 50, recycle in loop(), the in-use check, don't retain dispatched messages, and relative cost vs lambdas.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash IllegalStateException: This message is already in use came from a message stored in a retry list and re-sent after the first send.

questions.contextHtml: You are the tech lead for a photo-backup app (800k DAU). A new requirement: upload queue with sequential uploads, retry with backoff (5 s, 30 s, 2 min), cancel on user action, survive screen rotation, and keep working when the user leaves the app for up to ~10 minutes. A mid-level engineer proposes: a HandlerThread, postDelayed for retries, and a Handler shared across screens. Another suggests a started Service. Product says "uploads must eventually finish even if the app is closed, but nobody expects exact timing". Upload sizes: 3-25 MB, typically 5-40 pending, on cellular 25% of the time.
questions.promptHtml: How would you design it and what would you reject?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks the first tool they know (Handler or Service) without distinguishing in-process serialization from durable scheduling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must uploads survive process death and reboot? Does the user see progress (foreground, notification)? Are there network/battery constraints (unmetered only?)? Are uploads idempotent on the server? What are the targetSdk and minSdk?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd first agree on guarantees: "eventually completes, survives process death, constrained by network and battery, visible progress when active".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): (a) HandlerThread + postDelayed: serial and simple, but dies with the process and ignores Doze/standby for retries (uptime clock); (b) coroutine-based in-process queue (Channel + single consumer): great for foreground progress; still dies with the process; (c) WorkManager with constraints and backoff: durable, handles Doze, reboot and retries; (d) started Service: no guarantees after the background-start limits and API 26+ rules; foreground service only while the user is actively watching progress.
  4. How I'd verify each: Kill the process mid-upload (adb shell am kill), toggle airplane mode, force Doze (adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle), test on devices with aggressive battery managers; assert idempotent resume with server-side upload tokens.
  5. Root cause of the wrong instinct: conflating a threading primitive (Handler/Looper: ordering inside a live process) with a scheduling primitive (durable, constraint-aware, survives death).
  6. Fix (design): Persist the queue in Room (state, attempt, nextAttemptAt). Use WorkManager for durable execution with network constraint and exponential backoff (details belong to the WorkManager chunk); inside the worker use a coroutine and chunked/resumable upload. For foreground UX, observe progress via WorkInfo/Flow; if the user wants a long running visible transfer, use setForeground with a proper FGS type (verify per release). Keep a Handler only where a platform API demands it.
  7. Prevention: Failure-injection tests (kill, offline, low battery), idempotency keys, telemetry for time-to-complete and retry counts, a design doc stating guarantees.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't use a Handler for retry timing (uptime, process death); I wouldn't run a plain started Service (restricted since API 26); I wouldn't use AlarmManager exact alarms for retries (permissions and battery cost); I wouldn't use a foreground service unconditionally (user-visible notification, type/permission rules, and system timeouts).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product now says uploads must finish within 5 minutes of tap, even on Doze. → Use expedited work or a user-visible foreground service for the active window; be explicit that the OS can still defer expedited quota.
  • How do you keep strict ordering across retries? → Persist a sequence number; a single chained unique work (beginUniqueWork with APPEND), or a single worker that pulls the next item from the DB.
  • What does a Handler still do well here? → Serialize callbacks for the platform API you call if it needs a Looper, or debounce small UI refreshes in-process.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "just use a Service" uploader worked until Android 8 background limits; support tickets showed uploads stopping after the app was swiped away, and the fix was a database-backed queue plus WorkManager.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses Handler or Service without discussing process death or background limits.
  • Hire: separates in-process ordering from durable scheduling and picks WorkManager with persisted queue.
  • Strong hire: states guarantees up front, designs idempotency and resume, tests failure modes, and explains why each rejected option fails.
